chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Abdullah ibn Muskan, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
"There is no harm in praying in what is made of the wool of the animal that died (non-slaughtered), for the wool does not contain a soul."
Abdullah said: And Ali ibn Abi Hamzah told me that a man asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) while I was with him about a man who wears a sword and prays in it. He said: "Yes."

The man said: "Indeed, it has the kaymukh." He said: "And what is the kaymukh?" He said: "The skins of beasts, some of which are from slaughtered animals and some from non-slaughtered (dead) animals."
He said: "If you know that it is from a non-slaughtered animal, do not pray in it."

key_terms.الْكَيْمُخْتَ: A type of mixed leather or skin covering

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to pray in clothing or items made from the wool or skin of animals that died naturally?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between the carcass itself and its byproducts, ruling that wool from a *maytah* (non-slaughtered animal) is pure (*tahir*) because it is not considered to contain a soul (*ruh*), thereby permitting its use in prayer. Regarding mixed leather (*kaymukh*) used for sword sheaths, Imam al-Sadiq establishes the principle of *istishab* (presumption of purity) in cases of doubt, instructing that one only avoids prayer if they are certain the leather is from a non-slaughtered animal. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential preference for ease and the default purity of created materials unless proven otherwise.
